title: The tongue that did not burn
hookLine: a legend: after his cremation, Kumarajiva's tongue remained, proof his translations were true

cards: A translator's whole life's work rests on one question: did I get it right? Nobody can fully answer that for themselves. Readers decide, slowly, over generations.
Kumarajiva, the story goes, asked for a different kind of answer. Near the end of his life, he made a promise in front of his students, and the proof would come only after he was gone, in the fire.
Today, a legend: the tongue that did not burn.

teach.h: A PROMISE: MY TONGUE WILL NOT BURN.
teach.b: First, the promise. His biography tells it this way. Knowing he was dying, Kumarajiva spoke to the monks around him.
He said, in effect: if what I have translated does not betray the meaning of the teaching, then when my body is burned, my tongue will not burn. Second, the fire.
After his death, the story says, his body was cremated in the Buddhist way.
When the fire died down, his tongue remained, unburned. Third, what the story is saying.

teach.h: A CLAIM IN THE LANGUAGE OF WONDER.
teach.b: It makes its claim in the language of wonder. The tongue is the organ of speech, the thing that spoke every sentence of those translations. For it to survive the fire says, in a picture, that the words were sound.
His students, and the readers after them, could point to it. Fourth, how people hold it. Some Buddhists receive the story as a sign.
Historians read it as a legend that grew around a translator people already trusted.
Tradition says the tongue was enshrined in a pagoda, and a pagoda in the frontier town where he was once held is still linked to it.
Either way, the story sits at the very end of his life, after years of readers had already found his Chinese clear and faithful. Readers go on testing a translation slowly, in their own mouths.
The story gives his work one vivid image.

how: Chinese Buddhists retell the story of Kumarajiva's tongue as a sign of his faithfulness, and a pagoda associated with the relic is visited in western China.

games.q: the tongue that did not burn: tap the pairs.

s: the story is told as a sign the translations were faithful
he promised his tongue would not burn if he had not betrayed the meaning.
the legend came first, and then people began trusting his translations
the trust came first, from readers of his Chinese; the story of the fire comes at the end of his life.
historians and believers all read the story the same way
some Buddhists receive it as a sign; historians read it as a legend.

games.q: you're one of Kumarajiva's students, and he says his tongue will not burn if his translations are true. what do you do?
o: wait for the fire, and remember his words.
games.why: in the story, after the cremation, his tongue remained, and his students took it as proof his words were sound.

practice: Think of one thing you passed along this week: a message from a boss, a story from a friend, an instruction for a child.
Ask quietly whether you carried it faithfully, added anything or left anything out, with no judging, the way a careful translator reads a sentence twice. Then let it rest, and stay with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kumarajiva. The translator whose tongue, legend says, survived his cremation as a sign that his Chinese translations were faithful.

orig.note: Sanskrit: jihvā, the tongue, the organ of speech the legend says did not burn.
